title: Two birds on one tree
hookLine: two birds share one tree: one eats and grieves, one watches, and seeing it ends the grief
carry: the one who watches is on your branch
last: OM THE BOW, THE SELF THE ARROW.

lines: THE THIRD EPISODE. THE FOURTH COOKIE.
cards: Late at night: the third episode, the fourth cookie, the same feed scrolled twice. And sometimes, for a second, another part seems to sit a little above it all, noticing. Huh.
Look at me. That part doesn't scold, exactly. It just sees.
The Mundaka's third chapter opens with a picture of exactly that. It's older than the Upanishad itself. A tree, and two birds sitting in it.

teach.h: TWO BIRDS, CLOSE COMPANIONS, ONE TREE.
teach.b: Angiras opens his last chapter with this verse. Dva suparna sayuja sakhaya. Two birds, close companions, always together, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit.

teach.h: THE OTHER, NOT EATING, LOOKS ON.
teach.b: The other, not eating, looks on. Commentators read the tree as the body, and the life lived in it.
The bird that eats is the self as we usually know it, tasting every fruit, sweet and bitter, pleasure and pain, hungry for the next. The bird that watches doesn't eat at all. It isn't hungry.
It just shines there, looking on. Then the next verse tells the story. On that same tree, the eating bird sinks down, confused, and grieves, feeling helpless.

But when it sees the other, the Lord, content, and sees that one's greatness, its grief is gone. The eating bird doesn't have to fly to another tree. The watcher was on the same branch the whole time.
The verse is older than the Mundaka: it comes from a Rig Veda hymn of riddles. Here the schools of Vedanta part ways, honestly.

Advaita teachers read the two birds as one self seen two ways: the watcher is who the eater really is. Madhva's Dvaita school reads them as forever two, the soul and God, close companions who never merge.

Ramanuja's school reads them as two, inseparably joined, the soul as part of God's body, with God as its inner self. All of them keep the comfort of the verse, and one of Hinduism's warmest teachings: God isn't far off.

teach.h: THE LORD DWELLS IN THE HEART.
teach.b: The Gita says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being.
On your worst night, the eater isn't alone on the branch.

how: The two-birds verse is chanted in Vedic recitation, and Advaita, Dvaita and Vishishtadvaita teachers each explain the relation between the two birds in their own way.

the tree, read as the body and its life
the sweet fruit the eating bird tastes

Advaita reads one self; Dvaita and Ramanuja's school read two, closely joined.

games.q: you're the bird that eats. you've sunk down, confused and grieving. what frees you, in the Mundaka?
o: seeing the other bird, content, and its greatness.
games.why: when the eating bird sees the other, the Lord, content, and sees its greatness, its grief is gone.

practice: Let the eating bird be busy: thoughts, wants, a plan for later. Notice that something sees the pecking without eating or hurrying.

Many Hindus, when they're caught up, quietly say a name of God, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, a way of looking up to the other bird. If you don't pray, just rest in the noticing for a breath. When you get caught up again, look up again.

wordCard.voice: Suparna, a bird of fine wings. In the Mundaka, two birds sit on one tree: one eats the sweet fruit and grieves; the other looks on, content; and seeing it, the first is freed from grief.

orig.note: Sanskrit dvā suparṇā, two birds (literally, two of fine wings): Mundaka 3.1.1, from Rig Veda 1.164.20.
